options_ranked.title: Contract-Permitted Rebate Recapture and Promotion Reset
options_ranked.description: Restructure discretionary rebates and reduce promotional depth on Synthetic Blend Engine Oil at legally permitted reset windows, without changing locked anchor-account list prices or overriding committed rebates. Replace automatic volume rewards with incremental, contribution-protecting tiers. Apply promotion changes only to verified Synthetic Blend and Value-tier overlap; the supplied category totals do not establish that overlap. Defer incentives toward High Mileage or Full Synthetic until their realized margins exceed Synthetic Blend's 20.64%; no supplied product evidence establishes that superiority. Preserve within-threshold operating practices from 2026-006 through 2026-008 rather than imposing a business-wide reset. No well-performing product segment is identified for intervention or benchmark replication.
options_ranked.rationale: Customer profitability and price-volume-mix methods support intervening in net realization without automatically reaching for list-price increases. However, the supplied evidence does not establish rebate leakage, legal reset rights or the original assumed cost-versus-discount split; therefore the retained recovery range is a gated scenario rather than an evidenced forecast. External product switching is excluded from the quantified segment recovery.
options_ranked.time_to_value: Within 30–90 days where discretionary programs can change; otherwise at the next permitted renewal or rebate-reset date.

arguments_for: Customer profitability analysis supports replacing automatic rebates with incremental-volume tiers because Synthetic Blend has lost 7.14 margin points while anchor-account list prices are locked.
arguments_against: Price-volume-mix decomposition cannot attribute the observed decline to rebates from product margin totals alone, so assuming 2.8–4.2 points of recoverable leakage overstates the evidence.
key_questions: Which already-authorized rebate resets can the sales team execute without breaching effective-price protections or sacrificing profitable orders?

arguments_for: The client-confirmed net_revenue-to-gross_margin_pct relationship supports higher net realization as a margin mechanism without requiring manufacturing changes.
arguments_against: Cost-to-serve analysis warns that reduced promotional volume can leave fixed manufacturing costs spread over fewer units, offsetting rebate recovery.
key_questions: What shipment and production floors will prevent rebate changes from increasing unit conversion costs?

arguments_for: Portfolio participation analysis supports withdrawing uneconomic promotional support before making irreversible exits from a product still earning a reported 20.64% gross margin.
arguments_against: Rebate optimization preserves the existing portfolio and may not resolve enduring participation problems; moreover, High Mileage and Full Synthetic have no supplied margin benchmark.
key_questions: What realized contribution threshold will stop promotional support if the reset does not make targeted business worth serving?

implementation_triggers: Legal counsel confirms that the specific rebate or promotion is discretionary or reaches a permitted reset date.
Commercial leadership approves a contribution floor and customer-retention guardrail before issuing revised offers.
Incentives for another formulation activate only after its realized margin exceeds the targeted product's margin and customers accept the offer.
prerequisites: Preserve all locked list prices and contractually committed rebates; a rebate change is not automatically exempt from contractual pricing protections.
Use existing account economics to restrict changes to affected Synthetic Blend transactions and verified Value-tier overlap.
Exclude benefits from external product migration from the Synthetic Blend segment recovery claim.
Retain successful service and fulfillment practices associated with within-threshold periods rather than applying blanket changes.

impact_estimate.basis: The retained Stage 1 scenario targets 2.8–4.2 percentage points of Synthetic Blend Engine Oil's 7.14-point decline through permitted rebate recapture and within-segment promotion changes, implying a conditional segment margin of 23.44–24.84%, not an enterprise forecast.

key_assumptions.assumption: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil has a 7.14-point historical margin gap.
key_assumptions.provenance: The product change point reports 27.78% previously and 20.64% currently.

key_assumptions.assumption: A material share of rebates can be reset within the implementation horizon.
key_assumptions.provenance: Executed customer agreements permit the proposed reset dates and revised rebate tiers.

key_assumptions.assumption: Customers retain enough profitable purchases after incentives are reduced.
key_assumptions.provenance: Post-reset orders meet the approved revenue and gross-profit retention floors during the first two order cycles.

key_assumptions.assumption: Recoverable net-realization leakage is sufficient to support the retained impact scenario without relying on external product switching.
key_assumptions.provenance: Realized net prices and accrued rebates on eligible Synthetic Blend sales generate at least 2.8 margin points after volume and cost effects.

options_ranked.title: Delivered Base-Oil Cost Reset with Selective Supply Protection
options_ranked.description: Renegotiate delivered base-oil terms for Synthetic Blend Engine Oil, consolidate eligible purchase commitments and use supplier price locks or approved matched hedges only where they improve the approved delivered-cost outcome. Introduce cost-linked clauses on non-locked accounts or at permitted renewals, not through mid-quarter anchor-account list-price increases. Extend supplier terms to Conventional Engine Oil and Compressor Oil only where they share qualified inputs; their 6.61- and 5.86-point declines justify targeted eligibility, not an enterprise-wide redesign. Preserve within-threshold operating practices from 2026-006 through 2026-008. No unaffected product segment or internal product benchmark is supplied.
options_ranked.rationale: The client confirms that base-oil costs enter COGS and that COGS directly affects Gross Margin %, making delivered purchase-cost reduction a model-supported mechanism. The simultaneous product declines are consistent with, but do not establish, an input-cost shock. Hedge protection limits future exposure and cannot reverse costs already incurred; actual savings must come from contracted delivered economics and permitted commercial terms.
options_ranked.time_to_value: Initial benefits within 30–90 days as new purchases enter COGS; broader contract and inventory turnover effects over 3–12 months.

arguments_for: Contract-cycle leverage supports cost-linked clauses on non-locked accounts while preserving the explicit mid-quarter list-price protection on anchor accounts.
arguments_against: Willingness-to-pay segmentation warns that non-anchor customers may reject increases, so supply savings and commercial recovery cannot both be assumed at full value.
key_questions: Which eligible customers can accept cost-linked renewal terms without reducing their profitable purchases?

arguments_for: The client-confirmed base_oil_cost-to-cogs relationship and COGS margin identity support lowering delivered input costs as a direct operational intervention.
arguments_against: Procurement and hedging methods distinguish lower purchase cost from volatility protection: locking today's expensive inputs could preserve rather than repair compressed margins.
key_questions: Do proposed supply contracts reduce delivered cost after freight, premiums, inventory carrying costs and quality requirements?

arguments_for: Portfolio participation analysis favors improving a shared input platform before exiting several products whose declines may have a common, reversible cause.
arguments_against: Multi-period purchase commitments can entrench exposure to declining products; no supplied demand evidence establishes that the committed volumes remain attractive.
key_questions: What minimum purchase flexibility preserves the ability to reallocate the portfolio if engine-oil economics remain weak?

implementation_triggers: Qualified supplier offers beat the approved delivered-cost baseline after premiums, freight and inventory effects.
Treasury approves hedge instruments, exposure limits and purchase-volume matching before any commitment.
Non-locked contracts reach legally permissible repricing windows.
New inventory reaches production and cost recognition before recovery is credited to Gross Margin %.
prerequisites: Preserve anchor-account list-price locks throughout the quarter.
Require supplier quality qualification and maintain service continuity during allocation changes.
Limit commitments to defensible purchase volumes and retain contractual flexibility for portfolio changes.
Treat 60–70% base-oil attribution and 50–70% non-anchor coverage from Stage 1 as unverified assumptions, not established operating facts.

impact_estimate.basis: The retained Stage 1 scenario recovers 3.2–5.1 percentage points of Synthetic Blend Engine Oil's 7.14-point decline through lower delivered COGS and permitted non-locked contract changes, implying 23.84–25.74% segment margin; supply hedging alone does not establish this recovery.

key_assumptions.assumption: Reducing base-oil expense reduces COGS, holding other components constant.
key_assumptions.provenance: The client-confirmed causal context identifies Raw Materials/base oil as an additive component of COGS.

key_assumptions.assumption: Current qualified supplier terms contain achievable delivered-cost savings.
key_assumptions.provenance: Executed supplier offers and subsequent invoices show lower delivered cost for equivalent specifications.

key_assumptions.assumption: Purchase commitments and hedge volumes can be matched without material stranded exposure.
key_assumptions.provenance: Actual purchases remain within approved commitment bands through the first two replenishment cycles.

key_assumptions.assumption: Eligible contract changes and inventory turnover are sufficient to realize the retained recovery within the stated horizon.
key_assumptions.provenance: Recognized purchase savings and effective non-locked pricing deliver at least 3.2 Synthetic Blend margin points after inventory lag.

options_ranked.title: Revenue-Protected Portfolio Reallocation
options_ranked.description: Redirect discretionary sales capacity and replenishment investment from selected Synthetic Blend Engine Oil business only after replacement orders protect revenue and gross-profit dollars. Compressor Oil is a candidate for selling-capacity allocation because its current margin is 28%, above Synthetic Blend's 20.64%, but it is also underperforming by 5.86 points. First stabilize its delivered input and fulfillment economics through qualified supply and service terms; then redirect capacity against booked demand. Compressor Oil is not assumed to be a functional substitute for engine oil. Conventional Engine Oil, at 19.16%, is not a preferred destination. High Mileage, Full Synthetic and specialty formulations remain conditional candidates because their margins are absent. Preserve contracted anchor-account supply and within-threshold operating practices from 2026-006 through 2026-008; no healthy product benchmark is identified.
options_ranked.rationale: Portfolio participation should be judged on attainable margin levels and gross-profit dollars, not decline magnitude alone: Compressor Oil's 28% current margin exceeds Synthetic Blend's 20.64%, whereas Conventional's 19.16% does not. The intervention therefore replaces unconditional volume withdrawal with a replacement-order gate and an explicit destination-stabilization step. The high-severity revenue concern remains an execution exposure until replacement demand is contracted; increasing a ratio by shrinking profitable business is not counted as success.
options_ranked.time_to_value: Stage replacement orders within 90 days; phase capacity and inventory reallocation over 3–12 months after destination economics and demand gates are met.

arguments_for: Channel economics supports moving discretionary selling capacity toward a 28% margin opportunity rather than a 20.64% one when booked demand and contribution remain attractive.
arguments_against: Customer profitability analysis rejects assuming Compressor Oil can replace engine-oil purchases; customers, applications and order economics may differ materially.
key_questions: Which booked replacement orders preserve revenue and gross-profit dollars before Synthetic Blend replenishment is reduced?

arguments_for: Cost-to-serve and overhead-absorption methods support the explicit requirement to retain profitable production loading and stabilize destination economics before moving capacity.
arguments_against: Compressor Oil's 5.86-point deterioration indicates that reallocating toward it without repairing its cost exposure could reproduce the same problem.
key_questions: Which avoidable costs disappear with reduced Synthetic Blend participation, and which fixed costs remain on the retained portfolio?

arguments_for: Portfolio participation analysis correctly compares current margin levels, excludes lower-margin Conventional Engine Oil and conditions reallocation on replacement economics.
arguments_against: Category lifecycle analysis cannot classify the decline as structural from one year-to-date comparison; premature withdrawal could sacrifice profitable business during a cyclical cost shock.
key_questions: What contractual demand and contribution gates justify each reallocation tranche without requiring an unsupported structural-decline thesis?

implementation_triggers: Replacement orders are contracted before corresponding Synthetic Blend capacity or replenishment is withdrawn.
Destination economics are stabilized and exceed the origin margin after incremental selling, fulfillment and transition costs.
Each tranche preserves approved revenue, gross-profit-dollar and plant-loading floors.
Legal counsel confirms continued fulfillment of anchor-account supply and list-price obligations.
prerequisites: Use selling-capacity allocation rather than assumed product substitution where customer applications differ.
Stabilize Compressor Oil's declining economics before scaling it as a destination.
Require booked replacement revenue to offset withdrawn revenue and separately protect gross-profit dollars after stranded costs.
Define the Synthetic Blend-origin revenue cohort before launch; external replacement sales cannot be reported as recovery in the unchanged Synthetic Blend product segment.
Keep the intervention to a sales-and-inventory reallocation pilot; any plant exit or major capital change requires separate approval and cost scoring.

impact_estimate.basis: For a revenue-preserved cohort originating in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil, reallocating approximately 34–57% of revenue from its 20.64% margin to a stabilized 28% destination would yield approximately 2.5–4.2 percentage points against the original 7.14-point gap; this constructed cohort scenario is neither the enterprise KPI nor the remaining Synthetic Blend product's reported margin.
impact_estimate.scope_label: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil-origin revenue cohort

key_assumptions.assumption: Compressor Oil currently has a higher reported gross margin than Synthetic Blend Engine Oil, despite also deteriorating.
key_assumptions.provenance: The supplied product change points report Compressor Oil at 28%, down 5.86 points, and Synthetic Blend at 20.64%, down 7.14 points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Replacement demand exists at sufficient scale to preserve withdrawn revenue.
key_assumptions.provenance: Signed replacement orders cover the revenue scheduled for withdrawal before each allocation tranche.

key_assumptions.assumption: The destination margin can remain at least 28% as sales capacity is added.
key_assumptions.provenance: Incremental destination orders retain at least 28% realized gross margin after new supply and fulfillment terms take effect.

key_assumptions.assumption: Approximately 34–57% revenue reallocation is commercially and operationally feasible for the origin cohort.
key_assumptions.provenance: Approved allocation tranches achieve the specified replacement-revenue share without breaching capacity, contract or revenue floors.

key_assumptions.assumption: Stranded costs and transition expenses do not consume the apparent margin advantage.
key_assumptions.provenance: Realized gross-profit dollars after retained manufacturing costs and transition charges meet the approved pre-reallocation floor.

flagged_side_effects: Cutting Synthetic Blend participation before replacement orders are secured can reduce units sold and net revenue, leaving fixed costs behind and weakening both gross-profit dollars and the intended margin recovery.

commercial.framework: Price-Volume-Mix Decomposition with Customer Profitability Lens
commercial.hypothesis: Gross margin compression of 7.14 pp in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is driven by a combination of elevated base oil input costs (COGS driver) and/or aggressive discounting on this premium-positioned product line to defend volume in a competitive period. The 'Value' category segment showing -6.42 pp confirms downward mix pressure, suggesting customers are trading down or suppliers are conceding price to retain shelf space and order frequency.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil declined 7.14 pp (27.78% → 20.64%) YTD—the largest single product margin erosion, despite being positioned as a premium-margin tier
Conventional Engine Oil fell 6.61 pp (25.77% → 19.16%) in parallel, indicating systematic COGS pressure or coordinated pricing action across the lubricant portfolio, not isolated product issue
Value product_category segment dropped 6.42 pp (26.24% → 19.82%), signaling mix shift toward lower-margin tiers or volume-driven discounting to offset competitive pressure

operational.framework: Cost-to-Serve Analysis with Input-Cost Shock Diagnosis
operational.hypothesis: Gross margin compression of 7.14 pp in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is driven by a base oil cost shock (raw material inflation) that has not been offset by list price adjustment due to contractual price-lock constraints on anchor accounts. The -7.14 pp delta in the highest-margin synthetic blend product, paired with -6.61 pp in conventional (lower-margin baseline), indicates a proportionally larger absolute COGS increase hitting the premium product harder in percentage terms, consistent with unhedged commodity exposure in base oil procurement.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14 pp (27.78% → 20.64%) while Conventional fell 6.61 pp (25.77% → 19.16%), indicating both products absorbed similar absolute COGS increases but the synthetic blend—with structurally higher gross margin—suffered greater percentage point erosion, consistent with base oil cost inflation hitting both SKUs equally in absolute terms.

Value product category declined 6.42 pp (26.24% → 19.82%), aligning with the synthetic and conventional engine oil declines, suggesting a systemic input cost driver affecting the entire lubricant portfolio rather than product-specific discounting or volume mix shifts.

Compressor Oil also declined 5.86 pp, confirming the margin compression pattern is not isolated to engine oils but spans all base-oil-dependent products, pointing to a shared procurement or manufacturing cost input rather than customer-level pricing pressure or mix deterioration.

structural.framework: Portfolio Participation Analysis + Category Lifecycle Positioning
structural.hypothesis: Gross margin compression across engine oil portfolio (Synthetic Blend -7.14pp, Conventional -6.61pp) signals structural cost-input pressure rather than KPI-recoverable pricing variance. The synchronized decline across both premium and value tiers, combined with contractual price-lock constraints, indicates base_oil_cost and/or distribution_cost inflation is eroding blended margin faster than mix or volume can offset. This is a structural reallocation signal, not a fixable variance.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14pp (27.78% → 20.64%) and Conventional Engine Oil fell 6.61pp (25.77% → 19.16%) — parallel declines across the grade spectrum point to shared input cost driver, not product-specific commercial issue
Value category margin compressed 6.42pp (26.24% → 19.82%), indicating the margin loss is category-wide and structural, not isolated to a single SKU or customer segment
Compressor Oil also declined 5.86pp, confirming the signal spans multiple product lines — consistent with base oil cost inflation or distribution cost step-change rather than demand-side repricing

proposed_option.title: Surgical Rebate Restructuring + Selective Channel Mix Rebalancing
proposed_option.description: Reallocate margin recovery away from list-price repricing (blocked by contract lock) toward tiered rebate recapture on Synthetic Blend Engine Oil. Simultaneously audit and reduce promotional depth on lowest-margin 'Value' tier SKUs within this product family, redirecting volume incentives toward higher-margin formulations (High Mileage, Full Synthetic) where willingness-to-pay is defensible. Execute within Q1 renewal/rebate reset windows to avoid mid-quarter friction.
proposed_option.mechanism: Rebate restructuring bypasses the price-lock constraint by operating on net revenue post-contract, not on list price. By reducing rebate generosity on volume thresholds already being hit, you recover COGS-to-revenue ratio without touching contractual list terms. Simultaneously, shifting promotional spend from Value-tier discounts to High Mileage premiums restores blended margin mix (premium_mix_pct) while maintaining total order value and customer stickiness.

impact_estimate.basis: Synthetic Blend compression of 7.14 pp is split between estimated COGS/input cost pressure (~3.5–4.5 pp) and discounting/rebate leakage (~2.5–3.5 pp). Rebate recapture on 40–50% of the discounting component yields 1.0–1.75 pp direct recovery; mix rebalancing from Value to premium tiers adds 1.8–2.5 pp via higher-margin unit contribution. Conservative mid-range: 2.8–4.2 pp recovery in YTD blended gross margin %.

proposed_option.title: Base Oil Cost Hedging & Procurement Reset with Selective Contract Renegotiation
proposed_option.description: Conduct an immediate procurement audit to quantify the base oil cost increase YTD and map expiration dates on non-anchor customer contracts to identify renegotiation windows. Implement a forward-hedging strategy (futures or supplier lock-in) for Q3–Q4 base oil purchases to arrest further margin erosion, and prepare a phased price adjustment roadmap for non-locked accounts to recover 40–60% of the margin gap within 90 days.
proposed_option.mechanism: The margin fall is a direct COGS driver (confirmed causal relationship). Base oil is a direct component of COGS (confirmed). Unhedged commodity exposure in base oil procurement has inflated COGS without corresponding revenue adjustment due to price-lock constraints on anchor accounts. Hedging forward purchases and negotiating price increases on non-locked contracts directly reduces the COGS component and restores net revenue/COGS ratio balance, addressing the supply-side shock rather than masking it with internal process fixes.

impact_estimate.basis: Synthetic Blend margin fell 7.14 pp; if base oil cost increase accounts for 60–70% of the shock (typical for lubricant COGS structure), hedging forward purchases and capturing price increases on 50–70% of non-anchor volume would recover 3.2–5.1 pp within 90 days. Conventional and Compressor oils would see proportional recovery (6.6 pp and 5.9 pp potential respectively), validating the shared input-cost mechanism.

proposed_option.title: Portfolio Reallocation: Reduce Synthetic Blend Volume Participation; Redirect Mix to Higher-Margin or Lower-Input-Cost Alternatives
proposed_option.description: Given contractual price-lock constraints preventing mid-quarter list price recovery, the margin loss cannot be recovered through pricing within this quarter. Instead, reallocate sales effort and inventory allocation away from Synthetic Blend (highest absolute margin loss: -7.14pp) toward product lines with lower base oil cost exposure or higher structural margins (e.g., specialty formulations, high-mileage grades, or value-engineered conventional lines). This reframes the portfolio to defensible margin while cost normalization is monitored.
proposed_option.mechanism: Margin compression is driven by input cost inflation (base oil, distribution) that pricing cannot offset under current constraints. Reducing volume participation in high-cost-exposed products (Synthetic Blend, Conventional) and reallocating to lower-input-cost or higher-value alternatives directly lowers the blended COGS-to-revenue ratio without violating price-lock clauses. This trades volume for structural margin recovery.

impact_estimate.basis: Reallocation of 40–60% of Synthetic Blend volume to alternatives with 3–5pp higher margins (e.g., specialty or engineered formulations) can recover 2.5–4.2pp of blended margin without pricing action. Conservative estimate assumes partial volume recovery and mix headwinds; high estimate assumes faster customer acceptance of alternative products.
